fields.title: Esther
fields.subtitle: Ester, “Star”
fields.description: The story of a Jewish orphan who became queen of Persia and saved her people from destruction, read every year at the feast of Purim, and the one book of the Bible in which God is never named. A king’s banquets and a queen who refused to come; Mordecai at the palace gate; Haman the Agagite casting lots for the day the Jews would die; the words “Perhaps you have become queen for a time like this”, and Esther’s answer, “If I perish, I perish”; two banquets, a sleepless night, a gallows built for one man and used for another, and a month turned from grief into joy. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Esther about?
qa.answer: The rescue of the Jews of the Persian empire from a plot to destroy them. Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, becomes queen to King Ahasuerus without revealing her people. When the king’s chief official, Haman, gains a decree to kill all the Jews on a single day, Mordecai urges Esther to plead with the king, and she risks her life to do it. Haman is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai, a second decree allows the Jews to defend themselves, and the day of their intended destruction becomes the feast of Purim, still kept every year.

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Esther, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition credited it to the men of the Great Assembly, the council said to have followed Ezra, and some have suggested Mordecai, who is said to have recorded these events (9:20). The story is set in the reign of Ahasuerus, usually identified with Xerxes I, who ruled Persia from 486 to 465 BC, and most scholars date the book’s writing to the later Persian or early Greek period. Christians differ over how far to read it as straightforward history and how far as history told with a storyteller’s art.

qa.question: Why is God not mentioned in the book of Esther?
qa.answer: In the Hebrew text of Esther the name of God never appears, and there is fasting but no prayer, temple or mention of the law. Most Jewish and Christian readers have seen this silence as the book’s point: God is at work behind the scenes, through a queen’s courage, a king’s sleepless night and a string of events too well timed to be coincidence, even when no one names him. Mordecai’s hope that help would come “from another place” (4:14) has often been heard as a quiet hint of his care.

qa.question: What are the additions to Esther?
qa.answer: The ancient Greek translation of Esther contains six passages not found in the Hebrew, more than a hundred verses in all, including a dream of Mordecai, the texts of the king’s decrees, and prayers of Mordecai and Esther that name God freely. They are printed in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, where they belong to the deuterocanonical books. Protestant Bibles, and this edition, follow the Hebrew text.

qa.question: What is Purim?
qa.answer: The Jewish festival that celebrates the deliverance told in Esther, kept on the fourteenth of the month Adar, or the fifteenth in Jerusalem and other anciently walled cities. Its name comes from pur, “lot”, because Haman cast lots to choose the day of the Jews’ destruction (3:7; 9:24–26). The book commands it as a time of feasting and joy, of sending gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor (9:22). The scroll of Esther is read aloud in the synagogue, and the congregation drowns out Haman’s name with noise whenever it is read.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
For if you remain silent at this time, relief and rescue will come to the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s family will perish. And who knows? Perhaps you have become queen for a time like this.”

— Esther 4:14

Esther is one of the great stories of the Bible, and one of the strangest. It has a beautiful orphan who becomes queen, a wise guardian at the palace gate, a villain who builds a gallows for his enemy and is hanged on it himself, a king who cannot sleep, and a sudden, glorious reversal. It is told with suspense, irony and even humour. And in all its ten chapters, the name of God is never mentioned.

There is no prayer in it, though there is fasting. There is no temple, no sacrifice, no prophet, no miracle, and no mention of the law of Moses or the covenant. Yet the Jewish people have read it every year for more than two thousand years at the feast of Purim, and the church has kept it among the Scriptures. Its silence about God is not an accident. It is the book’s way of asking where God is when he cannot be seen, and of answering, without saying so, that he is everywhere.

Jews who stayed behind

The story is set in Susa, one of the capitals of the Persian empire, in the reign of King Ahasuerus. Most scholars identify him with Xerxes I, who ruled from 486 to 465 BC, and whose name in Persian lies behind the Hebrew form. The book describes him as ruling “127 provinces stretching from India to Cush”, from the Indus to the upper Nile. Greek historians tell of Xerxes’ great banquets, his failed invasion of Greece, and his queen Amestris, and scholars have long debated how the book’s account fits with theirs.

That places the story between the two halves of the book of Ezra: after the temple was rebuilt in Jerusalem, and before Ezra came from Babylon to teach the law. It is a story about the Jews who did not go home. Decades after Cyrus had let them return, most remained scattered across the empire, living as a minority among other peoples, under foreign law, at the mercy of the powerful. Esther is the story of what happened when those powers turned against them.

A book of banquets

The book is built around feasts. It opens with the king’s display of his wealth, “180 days in all”, followed by a seven-day banquet for everyone in Susa, with wine served in gold cups. Esther’s coronation is marked by a banquet. When the decree to destroy the Jews has gone out, the king and Haman “sat down to drink”. Esther exposes Haman at a banquet of her own making. And the book ends with the feasts of Purim, kept every year ever after. Feasting frames the story, and the reversal at its centre is a reversal of feasts: the drinking of the powerful turned into the joy of the rescued.

Vashti, and a king’s law

Chapter 1 shows us the world of the story. At the end of his banquet, the king, “in high spirits from the wine”, orders Queen Vashti to be brought in, wearing her crown, so that he can show off her beauty to his guests. She refuses. The king is furious, and his advisers fear that every wife in the empire will follow her example. So a law is issued, in “the laws of Persia and Media, which cannot be revoked,” that “every man should be master in his own house”.

The narrator does not comment, but the irony is plain. The most powerful man in the world cannot command his own wife, and his answer is to send letters to every province in every language. The king of this book is a man of vast power and very little judgement. That will matter. And so will the law that cannot be revoked.

Esther and Mordecai

To replace Vashti, young women are gathered from across the empire into the king’s harem. Among them is Hadassah, that is, Esther, an orphan raised by her older cousin Mordecai, “a Jew in the citadel of Susa”, a Benjaminite whose family had been carried into exile from Jerusalem. Hadassah is her Hebrew name and means “myrtle”; Esther is the name she is known by in the Persian court. On Mordecai’s instructions, she keeps her people a secret.

Esther wins the favour of everyone who sees her, and the king makes her queen. Some readers admire her poise; others are uneasy that a Jewish woman should enter a pagan king’s harem and conceal who she is, and Christian interpreters have read her early chapters in both ways. The book itself passes no verdict. It simply shows how little power she has over her own life, and how she uses what she is given.

The chapter ends with what looks like a loose end. Mordecai, sitting at the king’s gate, uncovers a plot by two of the king’s eunuchs to assassinate him, and tells Esther, who tells the king. The plotters are hanged, and the matter is “recorded in the book of the annals in the king’s presence.” Mordecai receives no reward. The reader files it away.

Haman the Agagite

In chapter 3 the king promotes Haman son of Hammedatha, “the Agagite”, and orders everyone to bow to him. Mordecai refuses. The book does not say why, except that “he had told them that he was a Jew.” But the names tell an old story. Agag was the king of the Amalekites, Israel’s ancient enemy, whom King Saul, son of Kish the Benjaminite, was commanded to destroy and spared (1 Samuel 15). Mordecai too is “son of Kish, a Benjaminite”. The quarrel at the king’s gate is the latest round of a very long war.

Haman is not content to punish one man. He looks “for a way to wipe out all the Jews throughout the kingdom of Ahasuerus.” He casts lots, the pur, to choose the day, and the lot falls on the thirteenth of Adar, eleven months away. Then he goes to the king with a speech that has been heard, in other words, many times since:

Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, “There is a certain people scattered and kept apart among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws are different from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king’s laws. It does the king no good to tolerate them.

— Esther 3:8

He offers a vast sum of silver. The king hands over his signet ring without even asking the name of the people: “The silver is yours, and the people too.” The decree goes out in every language to every province, ordering that all the Jews be killed on a single day, young and old, children and women. And the chapter ends with one of the most chilling sentences in Scripture:

At the king’s command the couriers went out in haste, and the law was issued in the citadel of Susa. The king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.

— Esther 3:15

“For a time like this”

Mordecai tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and goes through the city “crying out loudly and bitterly.” Across the empire the Jews mourn and fast. Esther, in the palace, hears only that her cousin is in sackcloth, and sends him clothes. Through a servant, Mordecai tells her everything and asks her to go to the king and plead for her people.

Esther’s answer is reasonable. Anyone who goes to the king uninvited may be put to death, unless he holds out his gold scepter, and the king has not called for her in thirty days. Mordecai’s reply, the verse that opens this introduction, is the heart of the book. He is sure the Jews will be rescued: help “will come to the Jews from another place”. He does not say where from. But he warns Esther that silence will not save her, and then he asks his great question: “And who knows? Perhaps you have become queen for a time like this.”

Esther’s answer marks the moment the orphan girl becomes the leader of her people. For the first time she gives Mordecai orders:

“Go and gather all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. My maids and I will fast in the same way. Then I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish.”

— Esther 4:16

A fast in the Bible goes with seeking God. The book does not say that anyone prays. But every reader knows what three days of fasting by a whole people in mortal danger means.

Two banquets and a sleepless night

On the third day Esther puts on her royal robes and stands in the inner court. The king holds out the scepter: “Even if it is half the kingdom, it will be given to you.” And Esther, instead of asking, invites the king and Haman to a banquet. At the banquet she invites them to another. The delay is maddening, and it is deliberate on the narrator’s part. Something is about to happen that Esther could not have arranged.

Haman goes home delighted, sees Mordecai at the gate, and boils over: “Yet none of this satisfies me as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.” His wife and friends advise him to build a gallows, about seventy-five feet high, and ask the king in the morning to hang Mordecai on it. Then comes the turning point of the whole book, in one short sentence: “That night the king could not sleep.”

The king has the annals read to him, and the reader finds that the loose end of chapter 2 was not loose after all. The record of Mordecai’s loyalty is read out, and the king learns that nothing has been done for him. At that very moment Haman arrives at the palace to ask for Mordecai’s death. The king asks him, “What should be done for the man the king delights to honor?” Haman thinks, “Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?”, and describes a royal parade. He then has to lead it himself, with Mordecai on the horse. Even Haman’s wife sees where things are going: “You will certainly fall before him.”

The reversal

At the second banquet Esther finally speaks. She asks for her life and the life of her people, “For I and my people have been sold to be destroyed, killed, and wiped out.” The king demands to know who has dared to do this, and Esther points across the table: “An adversary and an enemy! This evil Haman!” Within a few verses it is over:

So they hanged Haman on the gallows he had set up for Mordecai. Then the king’s anger died down.

— Esther 7:10

But the danger is not over. Haman’s decree, sealed with the king’s ring, cannot be revoked, and the thirteenth of Adar is still coming. So the king gives Mordecai the ring and lets him write a second decree, allowing the Jews in every city to gather and defend themselves against anyone who attacks them. Mordecai goes out from the king in royal robes, and the city that had been thrown into confusion now shouts for joy: “For the Jews it was a time of light and gladness, joy and honor.”

When the day comes, the book sums it up in two Hebrew words that could serve as its motto, “it was turned around”, translated here “the opposite happened”. The Jews overpower those who hated them. Chapter 9 records the killing of their enemies in Susa and the provinces, including Haman’s ten sons, and it is hard reading. Readers have responded in different ways. Some stress that the Jews act under the king’s decree, in self-defence against an attack the empire had authorised. Others are troubled by the numbers and by the second day of fighting that Esther asks for in Susa. The book itself repeats one detail three times, as if to make sure we notice it: “But they did not lay a hand on the plunder.” Saul had seized the plunder of the Amalekites, and lost his kingdom for it. This time, the war is not for gain.

Purim

The last part of the book explains the festival. The days of fighting become days of rest, “of feasting and joy, of sending gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor”, to remember “the month that was turned for them from grief into joy and from mourning into a holiday.” They are called Purim, after Haman’s lots: “That is why these days are called Purim, from the word Pur.” The man who cast lots to choose the day of destruction gave his name, in a sense, to the day of deliverance.

Jews still keep Purim on the fourteenth of Adar, or on the fifteenth in Jerusalem and other anciently walled cities, following the book’s distinction between Susa and the villages. The scroll of Esther is read aloud in the synagogue, and the congregation drowns out Haman’s name with noise every time it is read. The day before is kept by many as the Fast of Esther. The book closes briefly, with Mordecai second only to the king, a man who “worked for the good of his people and spoke up for the well-being of all their descendants.”

The hidden God

Why is God never named? The book has been read in many ways. Some have thought it a purely national story that only later found a place in Scripture, and its place in the canon was questioned by some in both synagogue and church; Martin Luther was famously uneasy with it. The ancient Greek translation added six passages, more than a hundred verses in all, including prayers of Mordecai and Esther that name God freely. These additions are printed in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; Protestant Bibles, like this one, follow the Hebrew.

But most readers, Jewish and Christian, have come to see the silence as the book’s point. The God of Esther does not part seas or send fire from heaven. He works through a queen’s courage and a king’s insomnia, through a forgotten record and a villain’s pride, through what looks like coincidence, until the coincidences become too many to be coincidences. The book does not tell us that God is at work. It lets us see it for ourselves. That is the way most believers experience God for most of their lives, and Esther is the book of the Bible for those times.

How to read Esther

Esther is a story, and it should be read the way a story is meant to be read: in one sitting, if possible, and preferably aloud. It takes less than an hour. Notice how carefully it is built: almost every scene in the first half has a mirror in the second, as the threats against the Jews come back on the heads of those who made them. Watch for the irony, which is everywhere, and for the small details that turn out to matter.

The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition credited it to the men of the Great Assembly, the council said to have followed Ezra; others have suggested Mordecai himself, since he is said to have “recorded these events” (9:20). Most scholars date it to the later Persian or early Greek period. Christians differ over whether to read it as straightforward history or as history told with the shaping and artistry of a great storyteller; its knowledge of Persian court life has impressed many readers.

As you read, keep asking the question the book never asks aloud: where is God in this? And then ask it of your own life.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices are worth knowing before you begin.

“From another place.” Mordecai’s words in 4:14 are kept as open as the Hebrew keeps them. Many readers hear in them a quiet hint of God’s care; the book never says so outright, and the translation does not say so either.

“Gallows.” The Hebrew word for what Haman builds is simply “tree” or “wooden pole”. The translation renders it “gallows”, the familiar term; the Persians also impaled their enemies on stakes, and that may be what is meant.

Months and measures. The months are named as the book names them, with their place in the year: Nisan is the first month, Adar the twelfth. Weights and sizes are given in modern equivalents, so Haman offers “about 375 tons of silver” and his gallows is “about 75 feet high”.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Esther 1
fields.body_html:
The feasts of King Ahasuerus

This is what happened in the days of Ahasuerus, the Ahasuerus who ruled over 127 provinces stretching from India to Cush, in those days, when King Ahasuerus sat on his royal throne in the citadel of Susa, in the third year of his reign, he gave a banquet for all his officials and servants. The army commanders of Persia and Media, the nobles and the officials of the provinces were present before him, while for many days, 180 days in all, he displayed the riches of his glorious kingdom and the splendor and honor of his greatness. When these days were over, the king gave a banquet lasting seven days for all the people present in the citadel of Susa, from the most important to the least, in the court of the garden of the king’s palace. There were white cotton curtains and violet hangings fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings on marble pillars, and couches of gold and silver on a mosaic floor of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl and precious stones. Drinks were served in gold cups, each one different from the others, and royal wine flowed freely, as the king’s generosity allowed. By the king’s rule for the drinking, no one was forced to drink, for the king had instructed all the officials of his household to let each guest do as he wished. Queen Vashti also gave a banquet for the women in the royal palace of King Ahasuerus.

Queen Vashti refuses to come

On the seventh day, when the king was in high spirits from the wine, he ordered Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar and Carcas, the seven eunuchs who served King Ahasuerus personally, to bring Queen Vashti before the king, wearing her royal crown, so that he could show off her beauty to the peoples and the officials, for she was very beautiful. But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king’s command, which the eunuchs brought her. The king became furious, and his anger burned within him. Then the king spoke to the wise men who understood the times, for it was the king’s practice to consult all who were experts in law and justice, and those closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena and Memucan, the seven officials of Persia and Media who had personal access to the king and held the highest rank in the kingdom: “According to the law, what should be done to Queen Vashti, since she did not obey the command of King Ahasuerus, which the eunuchs brought her?”

Memucan answered in the presence of the king and the officials, “Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king but also all the officials and all the peoples in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus. For what the queen has done will become known to all the women, and they will look down on their husbands. They will say, ‘King Ahasuerus ordered Queen Vashti to be brought before him, but she did not come.’ This very day the noble women of Persia and Media who have heard about the queen’s conduct will speak the same way to all the king’s officials, and there will be no end of contempt and anger. “If it pleases the king, let him issue a royal decree, and let it be written in the laws of Persia and Media, which cannot be revoked, that Vashti may never again come before King Ahasuerus. And let the king give her position as queen to another woman who is better than she is. When the king’s decree is proclaimed throughout his vast kingdom, all women will give honor to their husbands, from the most important to the least.” The king and the officials approved of this advice, and the king did what Memucan proposed. He sent letters to all the king’s provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, saying that every man should be master in his own house and should speak the language of his own people.

fields.title: Esther 2
fields.body_html:
A search for a new queen

Some time later, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had cooled, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what had been decreed against her. Then the king’s young attendants who served him said, “Let a search be made for beautiful young virgins for the king. Let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom to gather every beautiful young virgin to the harem in the citadel of Susa. Let them be put in the care of Hegai, the king’s eunuch who is in charge of the women, and let them be given their beauty treatments. Then let the young woman who pleases the king become queen instead of Vashti.” The king liked this advice, and he did so.

Mordecai and Esther

Now there was a Jew in the citadel of Susa named Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite, who had been carried into exile from Jerusalem among the captives taken away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had deported. He had brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle’s daughter, because she had neither father nor mother. The young woman had a lovely figure and was beautiful to look at. When her father and mother died, Mordecai took her in as his own daughter. So when the king’s command and his decree were proclaimed and many young women were gathered to the citadel of Susa and put in the care of Hegai, Esther too was taken to the king’s palace and put in the care of Hegai, who was in charge of the women. The young woman pleased Hegai and won his favor. He quickly provided her with her beauty treatments and her special food, and he gave her seven young women chosen from the king’s palace to serve her. Then he moved her and her attendants to the best place in the harem. Esther had not revealed her nationality or her family background, because Mordecai had told her not to. Every day Mordecai walked back and forth in front of the court of the harem to find out how Esther was and what was happening to her. Each young woman’s turn to go in to King Ahasuerus came after she had completed twelve months under the regulations for the women, since this was the full length of their beauty treatment: six months with oil of myrrh and six months with perfumes and cosmetics for women. This is how each young woman went in to the king: whatever she asked for was given to her to take with her from the harem to the king’s palace. She would go in the evening, and in the morning she would return to the second harem, in the care of Shaashgaz, the king’s eunuch who was in charge of the concubines. She would not go to the king again unless he was pleased with her and she was summoned by name. When the turn came for Esther, the daughter of Abihail, Mordecai’s uncle, who had adopted her as his daughter, to go in to the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai the king’s eunuch, who was in charge of the women, advised. And Esther won the favor of everyone who saw her. Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus in his royal palace in the tenth month, which is the month Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign. The king loved Esther more than all the other women, and she won his favor and approval more than any of the other virgins. So he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti. Then the king gave a great banquet for all his officials and servants, the banquet in honor of Esther. He also declared a release from taxes for the provinces and gave gifts with royal generosity. When the virgins were gathered together a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king’s gate. Esther still had not revealed her family background or her nationality, just as Mordecai had instructed her. She continued to follow Mordecai’s instructions as she had done when he was bringing her up.

Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king

In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king’s gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king’s eunuchs who guarded the doorway, became angry and plotted to assassinate King Ahasuerus. Mordecai learned of the plot and told Queen Esther, and Esther told the king, giving Mordecai the credit. The matter was investigated and found to be true, and both men were hanged on a gallows. And this was recorded in the book of the annals in the king’s presence.

fields.title: Esther 3
fields.body_html:
Haman seeks to annihilate the Jews

Some time later King Ahasuerus promoted Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite. He raised him high and gave him a seat above all the officials who served with him. All the king’s officials at the king’s gate used to kneel and bow down to Haman, because the king had ordered it for him. But Mordecai would not kneel or bow down. Then the king’s officials at the king’s gate said to Mordecai, “Why do you disobey the king’s command?” Day after day they spoke to him, but he would not listen to them. So they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai’s reason would be accepted, since he had told them that he was a Jew. When Haman saw that Mordecai did not kneel or bow down to him, he was filled with rage. But he thought it beneath him to lay hands on Mordecai alone, since they had told him who Mordecai’s people were. So Haman looked for a way to wipe out all the Jews throughout the kingdom of Ahasuerus, Mordecai’s people. In the first month, which is the month Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur, that is, the lot, in front of Haman, day by day and month by month, and it fell on the twelfth month, which is the month Adar.

Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, “There is a certain people scattered and kept apart among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws are different from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king’s laws. It does the king no good to tolerate them. If it pleases the king, let a decree be written to destroy them, and I will pay about 375 tons of silver into the hands of the officials in charge of the king’s business, to be put into the royal treasuries.” So the king took his signet ring off his hand and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews. The king said to Haman, “The silver is yours, and the people too. Do with them as you see fit.” The king’s scribes were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month, and a decree was written just as Haman commanded. It went to the king’s satraps, to the governors over each province, and to the officials of each people, to every province in its own script and every people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king’s signet ring. Letters were sent by couriers to all the king’s provinces, ordering that all the Jews be wiped out, killed and destroyed, young and old, children and women, on a single day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, and that their goods be taken as plunder. A copy of the text was to be issued as law in every province and published to all the peoples, so that they would be ready for that day. At the king’s command the couriers went out in haste, and the law was issued in the citadel of Susa. The king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.

fields.title: Esther 4
fields.body_html:
Mordecai urges Esther to plead for her people

When Mordecai learned all that had been done, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the middle of the city, crying out loudly and bitterly. He went only as far as the front of the king’s gate, because no one was allowed to enter the king’s gate dressed in sackcloth. In every province where the king’s command and his law arrived, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting, weeping and wailing. Many of them lay in sackcloth and ashes. When Esther’s maids and her eunuchs came and told her, the queen was deeply distressed. She sent clothes for Mordecai to wear so that he could take off his sackcloth, but he would not accept them. Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king’s eunuchs whom he had assigned to serve her, and she ordered him to go to Mordecai to find out what this was and why it was happening. So Hathach went out to Mordecai in the city square in front of the king’s gate. Mordecai told him everything that had happened to him, including the exact amount of silver Haman had promised to pay into the king’s treasuries for the destruction of the Jews. He also gave him a copy of the written law issued in Susa for their destruction, to show to Esther and explain to her. He told him to instruct her to go to the king, beg him for mercy, and plead with him for her people. Hathach went back and told Esther what Mordecai had said. Then Esther spoke to Hathach and gave him a message for Mordecai, “All the king’s officials and the people of the king’s provinces know that if any man or woman goes to the king in the inner court without being summoned, there is only one law: that person is to be put to death, unless the king holds out the gold scepter to them and spares their life. And I have not been summoned to come to the king for thirty days now.” When Esther’s words were reported to Mordecai,

he sent back this answer to Esther: “Do not imagine that because you are in the king’s palace you alone of all the Jews will escape. For if you remain silent at this time, relief and rescue will come to the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s family will perish. And who knows? Perhaps you have become queen for a time like this.” Then Esther sent back this reply to Mordecai, “Go and gather all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. My maids and I will fast in the same way. Then I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish.” So Mordecai went away and did everything Esther had instructed him.

fields.title: Esther 5
fields.body_html:
Esther’s banquet and Haman’s gallows

On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the palace, in front of the king’s hall. The king was sitting on his royal throne in the throne room, facing the entrance. When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won his favor, and he held out to her the gold scepter in his hand. So Esther came near and touched the tip of the scepter.

The king said to her, “What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? Even if it is half the kingdom, it will be given to you.” Esther replied, “If it pleases the king, let the king and Haman come today to a banquet I have prepared for him.” The king said, “Bring Haman at once, so that we may do as Esther asks.” So the king and Haman went to the banquet Esther had prepared. As they were drinking wine, the king said to Esther, “What is your petition? It will be granted to you. What is your request? Even if it is half the kingdom, it will be done.” Esther answered, “My petition and my request is this: If I have found favor with the king, and if it pleases the king to grant my petition and do what I request, let the king and Haman come tomorrow to the banquet I will prepare for them. Then I will do as the king has said.” Haman went out that day happy and in high spirits. But when he saw Mordecai at the king’s gate, and Mordecai neither stood up nor showed any fear of him, Haman was filled with rage against Mordecai. Nevertheless, Haman controlled himself and went home. He sent for his friends and his wife Zeresh. Haman boasted to them about his great wealth and his many sons, and about all the ways the king had honored him and raised him above the king’s officials and servants. Haman added, “What is more, Queen Esther let no one but me come with the king to the banquet she gave. And tomorrow she has invited me again, along with the king. Yet none of this satisfies me as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.” His wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, “Have a gallows built, about 75 feet high, and in the morning ask the king to have Mordecai hanged on it. Then go with the king to the banquet and enjoy yourself.” Haman liked the idea, and he had the gallows built.

fields.title: Esther 6
fields.body_html:
The king cannot sleep

That night the king could not sleep. So he ordered the book of records, the chronicles, to be brought, and they were read aloud to the king. There it was found written that Mordecai had exposed Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king’s eunuchs who guarded the doorway, who had plotted to assassinate King Ahasuerus. The king asked, “What honor or high rank has been given to Mordecai for this?” The young men who attended the king answered, “Nothing has been done for him.” The king said, “Who is in the court?” Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the palace to ask the king to have Mordecai hanged on the gallows he had set up for him. The king’s attendants told him, “Haman is standing in the court.” “Let him come in,” the king said. When Haman came in, the king asked him, “What should be done for the man the king delights to honor?” Haman thought to himself, “Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?” Haman answered the king, “For the man the king delights to honor, let royal robes be brought that the king himself has worn, and a horse that the king has ridden, one with a royal crown placed on its head, and let the robes and the horse be handed to one of the king’s most noble officials. Let them dress the man the king delights to honor, lead him on horseback through the city square, and proclaim before him, ‘This is what is done for the man the king delights to honor!’” Then the king said to Haman, “Hurry! Take the robes and the horse just as you have said, and do this for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king’s gate. Do not leave out anything you have proposed.” So Haman took the robes and the horse. He dressed Mordecai, led him on horseback through the city square, and proclaimed before him, “This is what is done for the man the king delights to honor!” Then Mordecai returned to the king’s gate, but Haman hurried home, grieving, with his head covered. Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. His advisers and his wife Zeresh said to him, “If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of Jewish descent, you will not get the better of him. You will certainly fall before him.” While they were still talking with him, the king’s eunuchs arrived and hurried Haman off to the banquet Esther had prepared.

fields.title: Esther 7
fields.body_html:
Esther names her enemy

So the king and Haman came to feast with Queen Esther. On this second day, as they drank wine, the king again asked Esther, “What is your petition, Queen Esther? It will be granted you. What is your request? Even if it is half the kingdom, it will be done.” Queen Esther answered, “If I have found favor with you, my king, and if it pleases the king, grant me my life: that is my petition. And grant me my people: that is my request. For I and my people have been sold to be destroyed, killed, and wiped out. If we had only been sold as slaves, men and women, I would have kept quiet, because such trouble would not be worth disturbing the king.”

King Ahasuerus demanded of Queen Esther, “Who is he? Where is the man who has dared to do such a thing?” Esther said, “An adversary and an enemy! This evil Haman!” Then Haman was terrified before the king and queen. In his rage the king got up from the wine feast and went out into the palace garden. But Haman stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he saw that the king had already decided on his ruin. Just as the king returned from the palace garden to the banquet hall, Haman was falling on the couch where Esther was reclining. The king said, “Will he even assault the queen while I am in the house?” As soon as the words left the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face.

Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs attending the king, said, “There is also the gallows Haman made for Mordecai, the man who spoke up for the king. It stands at Haman’s house, about 75 feet high.” The king said, “Hang him on it!” So they hanged Haman on the gallows he had set up for Mordecai. Then the king’s anger died down.

fields.title: Esther 8
fields.body_html:
Mordecai receives the king’s signet ring

That same day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai came into the king’s presence, because Esther had told how he was related to her. The king took off his signet ring, which he had taken back from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther put Mordecai in charge of Haman’s estate.

Esther pleads again for her people

Esther spoke to the king once more. She fell at his feet, weeping, and begged him to undo the evil of Haman the Agagite, the scheme he had devised against the Jews. The king held out the golden scepter to Esther, and she rose and stood before the king. She said, “If it pleases the king, and if I have found favor with him, and if the matter seems right to the king, and if I am pleasing to him, let an order be written to revoke the letters devised by Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, which he wrote to destroy the Jews in all the king’s provinces. For how can I bear to see the disaster that is coming on my people? How can I bear to see my family destroyed?”

A new decree written to every province

King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, “Look, I have given Haman’s estate to Esther, and he has been hanged on the gallows because he tried to attack the Jews. Now you write whatever you think best concerning the Jews, in the king’s name, and seal it with the king’s signet ring. For a decree written in the king’s name and sealed with the king’s ring cannot be revoked.” So the king’s scribes were summoned at that time, on the twenty-third day of the third month, the month of Sivan. Everything Mordecai ordered was written down, to the Jews and to the satraps, the governors, and the officials of the 127 provinces stretching from India to Cush. It was written to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, and to the Jews in their own script and language. Mordecai wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed it with the king’s signet ring, and he sent the letters by mounted couriers riding swift horses bred for the royal service, saying that the king allowed the Jews in every city to gather and defend their lives, and to destroy, kill, and wipe out any armed force of any people or province that might attack them, together with their children and women, and to plunder their goods, on a single day in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar. A copy of the text was to be issued as law in every province and made known to all the peoples, so that the Jews would be ready on that day to take revenge on their enemies. The couriers, riding the royal horses, went out in haste, urged on by the king’s command. And the decree was issued in the citadel of Susa.

Light and gladness for the Jews

Mordecai left the king’s presence wearing royal robes of blue and white, a large gold crown, and a cloak of fine linen and purple. And the city of Susa shouted for joy. For the Jews it was a time of light and gladness, joy and honor. In every province and in every city, wherever the king’s command and his decree arrived, there was gladness and joy among the Jews, with feasting and a holiday. And many people of the land became Jews, because fear of the Jews had come over them.

fields.title: Esther 9
fields.body_html:
The day that was turned around

In the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, on its thirteenth day, the king’s command and his decree were due to be carried out. On the very day when the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them, the opposite happened: the Jews overpowered those who hated them. The Jews gathered in their cities throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to attack those who were seeking to harm them. No one could stand against them, because fear of them had fallen on all the peoples. All the officials of the provinces, the satraps, the governors and the king’s administrators supported the Jews, because fear of Mordecai had fallen on them. For Mordecai was powerful in the king’s palace, and his fame spread through all the provinces; the man Mordecai grew more and more powerful.

The Jews struck down all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them, and they did as they pleased to those who hated them. In the citadel of Susa the Jews killed and destroyed 500 men. They also killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai and Vaizatha, the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. But they did not lay a hand on the plunder. That same day the number of those killed in the citadel of Susa was reported to the king.

The king said to Queen Esther, “In the citadel of Susa the Jews have killed and destroyed 500 men and the ten sons of Haman. What must they have done in the rest of the king’s provinces! Now what is your petition? It will be granted you. What else do you ask? It will be done.” Esther answered, “If it pleases the king, let the Jews in Susa be allowed to act tomorrow too, as today’s decree allows, and let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows.” So the king ordered that this be done. A decree was issued in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged. The Jews in Susa gathered again on the fourteenth day of the month Adar and killed 300 men in Susa. But they did not lay a hand on the plunder. Meanwhile the rest of the Jews in the king’s provinces gathered to defend their lives, and they had rest from their enemies. They killed 75,000 of those who hated them, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder. This was on the thirteenth day of the month Adar. On the fourteenth they rested and made it a day of feasting and joy. But the Jews in Susa had gathered on both the thirteenth and the fourteenth, so they rested on the fifteenth and made it a day of feasting and joy. That is why the Jews of the villages, who live in unwalled towns, keep the fourteenth day of the month Adar as a day of joy and feasting, a holiday, when they send gifts of food to one another.

Mordecai’s letter and the days of Purim

Mordecai recorded these events, and he sent letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far, to require them to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month Adar every year, as the days when the Jews got rest from their enemies, and as the month that was turned for them from grief into joy and from mourning into a holiday. They were to make them days of feasting and joy, of sending gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor. So the Jews made a custom of what they had begun to do, and of what Mordecai had written to them. For Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them. He had cast Pur (that is, the lot) to crush and destroy them. But when Esther came before the king, he gave orders in writing that the evil plan Haman had plotted against the Jews should fall back on his own head, and Haman and his sons were hanged on the gallows. That is why these days are called Purim, from the word Pur. And so, because of everything written in this letter, and because of what they had seen and what had happened to them, the Jews made it a binding custom for themselves, for their descendants and for all who joined them, that without fail they would keep these two days, as it was written and at the appointed time every year. These days are to be remembered and kept in every generation, by every clan, in every province and in every city. These days of Purim must never disappear from among the Jews, and the memory of them must never fade among their descendants.

Then Queen Esther, the daughter of Abihail, along with Mordecai the Jew, wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter about Purim. Mordecai sent letters to all the Jews in the 127 provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, with words of peace and truth, to confirm these days of Purim at their appointed times, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had ordered them, and as they had taken on themselves and their descendants the keeping of fasts and lamenting. Esther’s command confirmed these rules for Purim, and it was written down in the book.

fields.title: Esther 10
fields.body_html:
The greatness of Mordecai

King Ahasuerus imposed tribute on the mainland and on the coastlands of the sea. All his powerful and mighty deeds, and the full account of the high rank to which the king raised Mordecai, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia. For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus. He was great among the Jews and well liked by his many fellow Jews, because he worked for the good of his people and spoke up for the well-being of all their descendants.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus. He was great among the Jews and well liked by his many fellow Jews, because he worked for the good of his people and spoke up for the well-being of all their descendants.

— Esther 10:3

Esther ends quietly. The enemies are gone, the feast is fixed in the calendar, and the last we hear is of a Jew who rose high in a foreign court and used his place for the good of his people. The book that began with a king showing off his riches ends with a servant spending his influence on others. That too is a reversal.

The question the book leaves with you

The book never asks where God is. It leaves the reader to ask, and to notice the answer. An orphan becomes queen just before she is needed. A forgotten good deed lies in the king’s annals. On the one night that matters, the king cannot sleep, and the book that is read to him is the one that mentions Mordecai. Haman is in the courtyard at that very moment, and is hanged on his own gallows. No one in the story says, “God did this.” But by the end, no reader can quite believe that no one did.

Wisdom had already put it in a single line: “The lot is tossed into the lap, but how it falls is decided by the LORD.” Haman cast his lots to choose a day for destruction. He did not know who decides how they fall.

The question Esther leaves, then, is really two questions. The first is whether you can trust a God you cannot see, in a world where his name is not spoken and his hand is not obvious. The second is Mordecai’s question to Esther, and it is put to every reader: “And who knows? Perhaps you have become queen for a time like this.” Esther could have kept silent and hoped. Instead she fasted, risked her life, and went in to the king. Providence, in this book, works through human courage, not around it.

Where the story points

The apostle Paul never mentions Esther, but he writes the sentence that sums up her book:

“We know that, for people who love God, all things work together and lead to good. They are the ones called in keeping with his purpose.”

— Romans 8:28

Christian readers have also seen in Esther a shadow of a greater rescue. A whole people stood under a sentence of death that could not be revoked. One of their own, raised to a place near the king, went in on their behalf at the risk of her life, saying, “If I perish, I perish.” The sentence was not cancelled; a second decree was given that turned the day of death into a day of life. And the enemy who had plotted their ruin fell into the very trap he had built.

The New Testament tells of one who did not only risk death for his people but died for them, and rose again. He did not need to wait for the scepter to be held out. The letter to the Hebrews says of him that “he is always alive to plead on their behalf.” And the greatest reversal of all is the one the church celebrates at Easter, when the cross, the instrument of death, became the means of life. The book of Esther says it in its own way: a month “turned for them from grief into joy and from mourning into a holiday.”

Where to go from here

Esther has comforted God’s people in many dark times, and some of what it has inspired is in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On Esther and God’s faithfulness. Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, whose chapter “Esther: God’s Faithfulness” reads the book as a picture of God’s unseen care for his people.
  • On “a time like this” (Esther 4:14). Portraits of Courage – Corrie ten Boom, an Ochorus Original, whose chapter “May 1940” opens with Mordecai’s words to Esther and tells of the German invasion of the Netherlands, when a watchmaker’s family in Haarlem faced their own time like this.
  • On the story of the return. The Big Story, an Ochorus Original, whose chapter “Coming Home” tells the story of Ezra 1, Nehemiah 8 and Esther 4 together.
  • On providence. Thomas Watson’s All Things for Good, on Romans 8:28 and how even the worst things work for good to those who love God; and John Calvin’s Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 17, “Use to Be Made of the Doctrine of Providence”, on finding comfort in the God who governs all things.
  • For younger readers. Tell Me the Story – Book 3: Kings and Prophets, whose chapter “Queen Esther” tells the story for children to hear at bedtime; and Rooted – 30 Days with God for Youth – Book 6, whose “Day 21 — For Such a Time as This” is a devotion on Esther 4:14.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Esther in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

Then read the book again, perhaps aloud, and listen for the name that is never spoken. It is there in the silence, and in the courage of a young woman who decided that her people’s lives were worth more than her own:

“Go and gather all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. My maids and I will fast in the same way. Then I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish.”

— Esther 4:16
